one_liner: Book example: CRTP base-class call versus a virtual call through a base pointer; about 5.8x per 32-call loop.
what_it_does: Chapter08/01_function_call.C is a Google Benchmark file that times 32 calls per iteration of a trivial f(int) that adds to a member counter, through four class designs: a plain non-virtual class, a virtual function called through a base pointer, a CRTP base whose f() static_casts this to the derived type and calls its f(), and a second CRTP variant called through a free apply() template. It is teaching code for the CRTP idiom, not a library: you adopt the pattern by making the base a class template parameterised on the derived class, which changes the class hierarchy and every place that names the base.
how_it_is_fast: CRTP (curiously recurring template pattern) resolves the call at compile time: B<D>::f() does static_cast<D*>(this)->f(i), so there is no vtable lookup and the compiler can inline the derived body. In this benchmark the inlined body lets the compiler fold the 32 additions per iteration, so the reported gap measures inlining and loop folding as much as the cost of an indirect call. The plain non-virtual class runs at the same speed as the CRTP versions, which shows the CRTP layer itself costs nothing once inlined.
when_to_use: Hot loops calling small customisation-point methods where the concrete type is known at compile time and the virtual call blocks inlining.
Mixin-style code reuse (shared base logic calling derived hooks) where you never need a container of heterogeneous base pointers.
Template-heavy libraries that already instantiate per type, where one more template parameter on the base costs nothing extra in code organisation.
As a runnable starting point for measuring virtual versus static dispatch on your own compiler and CPU, since the repo carries the Google Benchmark source.
when_not_to_use: When the concrete type is chosen at run time or objects of different derived types must live behind one base pointer or in one container; CRTP gives each derived class an unrelated base type B<D>.

When the method body does real work: the 5.8x gap comes from a one-add body, and the dispatch share shrinks as the body grows (the per-call figures are about 0.28 ns virtual and 0.05 ns CRTP, derived from the relayed numbers).

When the compiler can already devirtualize the virtual call (final classes, a dynamic type visible at the call site, LTO); the gap may be small or absent and the extra template machinery buys nothing.
When code size or compile time matters: every derived class instantiates its own base, and the base must live in headers.
As evidence for a specific speedup on your platform: compiler, flags and CPU are not stated anywhere in the repo, and the figures are the book's own run.

integration.form: source-drop (language idiom; example classes inside a single Google Benchmark .C file)
integration.dependencies: none for the idiom; the benchmark file needs Google Benchmark (version not stated); the repo has no CMakeLists.txt, Makefile or other build files in Chapter08 or at the root
integration.min_toolchain: the CRTP idiom needs only class templates (C++98); the benchmark's range-for over benchmark::State needs C++11 plus whatever Google Benchmark requires; README lists GCC, Clang or Visual Studio
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (dispatch idiom, no shared state); the example objects are not synchronised

gotchas: The benchmarked CRTP base uses the same name f for the base and derived method; if a derived class forgets to define f, static_cast<D*>(this)->f(i) finds B<D>::f and recurses without end. The repo's own Chapter08/02_bad_crtp.C shows this case, and 03_good_crtp.C fixes it by naming the derived hooks f_impl and g_impl so a missing hook fails to compile or falls back to a base default.

static_polymorphism::B keeps a virtual destructor, so the CRTP object still carries a vtable pointer; the static_polymorphism1 variant drops it, and deleting a derived object through a B<D>* without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour (that variant uses a stack object to avoid it).

Harness: BM_dynamic allocates new D in the same function, so the compiler sees the dynamic type and may devirtualize the call (the about one cycle per virtual call implied by the relayed 9.04 ns per 32 calls suggests it did, at least speculatively; inferred, not compiled). Nothing opaque runs inside the timed loop and the counter is only read through DoNotOptimize after the loop, so the inlined rows fold the 32 adds.

Harness: the counters are signed int and the loop adds 32 increments per iteration with no reset; the summed i_ passes INT_MAX after about 2,000 iterations in every row, and at the iteration counts Google Benchmark picks for a 1.5 ns body (hundreds of millions) i itself overflows too, which is undefined behaviour. It likely does not change the timing in practice, but the code is not well-defined as written.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against the Bendersky CRTP-versus-virtual sibling (about 6x on an Intel i7-4771, code inline in a 2013 post with no license seen), pick this one when you want MIT-licensed, runnable Google Benchmark source to rerun on your own machine; read Bendersky for the original inlining argument and a stated CPU. The chapter 1 sibling from the same repo covers replacing dynamic_cast type tests with a virtual call, a different decision.
verified_claims_summary: Reported by the book and relayed by the seed lead, not shown anywhere in the repo: 9.04 ns per iteration of 32 virtual calls through a base pointer against 1.55 ns for the CRTP call and 1.60 ns for the plain non-virtual call, about 5.8x (derived). Compiler, flags, Google Benchmark version and CPU are not stated; the repo holds only the benchmark source, which matches that description.
status_note: Stale publisher companion repo (last commit 2024-08-29, a README errata update; the benchmark file was added 2023-02-22 and no code has changed since mid-2023), MIT-licensed and copyable, but it is a teaching example of an idiom rather than a component to vendor.
